\paragraph{Learning from Noisy Labels.}
Our silver-label pipeline produces labels with systematic noise from LF disagreement, connecting to the broader noisy label learning literature.
\citet{han2018coteaching} introduce co-teaching, where two networks train simultaneously and select small-loss samples for each other, mitigating confirmation bias in the presence of label noise.
\citet{li2020dividemix} extend this with DivideMix, combining sample selection via a Gaussian mixture model with semi-supervised learning on discarded samples.
These methods assume instance-level noise that is approximately class-conditional; our setting differs in that noise is structurally correlated---LFs introduce temporal block noise (entire stagnation episodes may be mislabeled) rather than independent per-sample flips.
Our confidence-based stratification (conf${\geq}$2 vs.\ conf${=}$1) serves an analogous role to sample selection: high-confidence windows train the detector, while ambiguous windows are effectively down-weighted.
This connection suggests that co-teaching or mixture-model selection over LF agreement patterns could complement majority vote aggregation in future work.

\paragraph{Label Leakage and Goodhart Effects.}
When evaluation targets are derived from the same signals used as input features, the resulting metric can overstate true performance---a phenomenon formalized as label leakage \citep{kaufman2012leakage}.
In our setting, structural features overlap with LF inputs (e.g., repetition ratios feed both the cmd\_rep LF and the structural classifier), producing the 0.995 in-domain F1 that we flag as circular (\S\ref{sec:circular}).
This overlap also instantiates a form of Goodhart's Law \citep{manheim2018goodhart}: optimizing a classifier against LF-derived silver labels risks learning to reconstruct LF voting patterns rather than detecting genuine stagnation.
We mitigate this through cross-agent transfer evaluation, where the model is tested on a different agent's LF distribution, and through a pending human-annotated gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}).
Recent programmatic weak supervision work addresses related concerns: \citet{maheshwari2022spear} propose SPEAR, a semi-supervised data programming framework that jointly learns LF reliability and a downstream model, reducing sensitivity to LF design choices---a direction that could help decouple structural classifiers from their LF-derived training signal.

4	We presented a systematic study of progress stagnation detection in LLM coding agents, comparing structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge approaches.
5	Three findings emerge.

7	First, structural features dominate zero-shot cross-agent transfer.
8	Thirty lightweight features achieve 0.9951 in-domain and 0.9674 cross-agent macro-F1, outperforming neural probes by 36.9\,pp and substantially exceeding zero-shot LLM judges in zero-shot settings.

11	
12	Second, labeling functions exhibit agent-specific temporal dynamics.
13	Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent but lags by 3.32 steps on OpenHands.

15	Label version bias---not LF noise---was the dominant cross-agent transfer bottleneck.
16	
17	Third, no label model improves over majority vote.
